sentences.text: Philosophy of mathematics asks what numbers, sets, structures, and proofs are and how mathematical knowledge is possible.
The apparent necessity and abstractness of mathematical truths create problems for theories of knowledge based exclusively on sensory observation.
Gottlob Frege and Bertrand Russell sought logical foundations for mathematics.
David Hilbert developed a programme centered on formal systems and consistency proofs.
L. E. J. Brouwer's intuitionism connects mathematics with constructive mental activity and questions some classical proof principles.
Kurt Gödel's incompleteness results placed limits on certain formalist ambitions.
Mathematical platonists treat mathematical objects as mind-independent.
Nominalists seek to avoid such commitments, while structuralists describe mathematical objects through positions and relations within patterns.
Paul Benacerraf's challenges concern both how abstract objects could be known and how numbers should be identified.
Set theory studies infinite collections and the axioms governing them.
Questions about the continuum hypothesis and large cardinals raise issues about independence, truth, and the justification of axioms.
Category theory offers a different language for relationships and structures, though its role as a foundation remains contested.
Mathematical knowledge depends on proof, but philosophers examine the roles of diagrams, examples, intuition, explanation, and computer verification.
Formal proof assistants and computer-assisted proofs invite questions about trust, surveyability, and the social organization of mathematical expertise.

Ancient Greek mathematical argument, Indian work on numeration and algebra, Chinese mathematical problem-solving, and mathematical traditions in the Islamic world developed varied techniques and standards of demonstration.
These histories complicate the idea that mathematics has one uninterrupted methodological origin or a single timeless style of proof.
Why does mathematics apply so effectively to the physical world?
Does mathematical explanation in science support realism about abstract entities?
Philosophers also examine probability, mathematical beauty, the epistemology of diagrams, and the relationships among logic, computation, and mathematical understanding.

new_text.text: Chapter 4 of Deleuze’s Difference and Repetition (1968; trans. Paul Patton, 1994, whose pages are cited here) turns to the differential calculus to set out its account of Ideas, opposing dx, the symbol of difference, to the symbol of contradiction (p. 170).

claims.excerpt: the symbol of difference [Differenzphilosophie] to that of contradiction

new_text.text: It is a mistake, he writes, to tie the value of dx to the existence of infinitesimals, and equally a mistake to refuse it any ontological or epistemic value, since there is “a treasure buried within the old so-called barbaric or pre-scientific interpretations” of the calculus (p. 170).

claims.by: Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (trans. Patton, 1994), owner's copy, ch. 4 text file, p. 170
claims.excerpt: tie the value of the symbol dx to the existence of infinitesimals

new_text.text: He finds that treasure in three readers whom he calls “a Leibniz, a Kant and a Plato of the calculus”: Salomon Maimon (1790), Hoene Wronski (1814) and Jean Bordas-Demoulin (1843) (pp. 170–1).

claims.by: Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (trans. Patton, 1994), owner's copy, ch. 4 text file, pp. 170–1
claims.excerpt: A Leibniz, a Kant and a Plato of

new_text.text: On this reading dx is undetermined in relation to x, the relation dy/dx is determinable, and its values are determined, so that “dx is the Idea” (p. 171); Ideas form a system of differential relations between reciprocally determined elements (pp. 173–4).

claims.by: Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (trans. Patton, 1994), owner's copy, ch. 4 text file, p. 171
claims.excerpt: In short, dx is the Idea

new_text.text: Through Maimon he rereads Kant’s example that the straight line is the shortest: “shortest” becomes an Idea that internalizes the difference between straight and curved, where Kant had a schema of the imagination standing between concept and intuition (p. 174).

claims.by: Deleuze, Difference and Repetition (trans. Patton, 1994), owner's copy, ch. 4 text file, p. 174
claims.excerpt: The shortest is not a schema but an Idea

new_text.text: Deleuze sets out the modern reading, on which the limit involves only static considerations and set theory gives the calculus a strictly finite interpretation (p. 176).

claims.excerpt: the notion of limit has lost its phoronomic character

new_text.text: Of the two old alternatives he says the first, whether differentials are real or fictive, collapses, since differentials “express the nature of a problematic as such”; the second, between infinite and finite representation, perhaps collapses as well, and modern mathematics, he writes, leaves an antinomy, since its finite interpretation presupposes an axiom of infinity (p. 178).

new_text.text: Following Albert Lautman, he takes a problem to differ in kind from its solutions, to transcend them and to be immanent in them; the calculus is “an entirely mathematical instrument,” yet “Problems are always dialectical” and what is mathematical “are the solutions” (pp. 178–9).

new_text.text: He adds that the calculus is one mathematical expression of problems among others, and credits Abel and Galois with methods in which solvability follows from the form of the problem (pp. 179–80).

new_text.text: Henry Somers-Hall’s guide (2013) explains that Deleuze rejects both the infinitesimal reading and the modern reading by limits, which gives the differential only a formal meaning, and so “returns to the metaphysical readings of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries”; he links the result to Plato’s divided line, since Deleuze sets a dialectic over mathematics while keeping the calculus inside mathematics.

claims.excerpt: Deleuze, however, holds that this reading is also a mistake
When we looked at Plato’s simile of the divided line

new_text.text: Daniel W. Smith reads the calculus as a model: Deleuze “finds in the calculus a model of pure difference” and uses it to develop “a properly philosophical concept of difference” (Smith 2020, p. 43); in another essay, “Axiomatics and Problematics,” Smith sets the problematics Deleuze favours, which moves from a problem to the events that condition it, against axiomatics, which moves from axioms to theorems.

claims.by: Smith 2020, Deleuze and Guattari Studies 14.1, p. 43
claims.excerpt: Deleuze finds in the calculus a model of pure difference
in problematics a deduction moves from the problem

new_text.text: Daniela Voss’s SEP entry likewise reads the dx passage as aimed at “a properly philosophical concept of difference,” and holds that Deleuze knew of the finitist revolution in the calculus, which Sokal and Bricmont (1999) had doubted.

claims.excerpt: Deleuze was aware of the finitist revolution
despite Sokal and Bricmont’s 1999 intimations otherwise

new_text.text: Simon Duffy traces Deleuze’s sources in the history of mathematics in detail: his chapter on Lautman (2009) says Deleuze understands the calculus essentially as a “calculus of problems,” and Aden Evens’s review of Duffy’s Deleuze and the History of Mathematics (2013) reports that Deleuze “redeploys” Weierstrass’s mathematics of singularities as ontology, a reading that, Evens objects, “pins the discussion to a mathematical discourse.”

claims.excerpt: Deleuze understands the differential calculus essentially as a ‘calculus of problems’
it pins the discussion to a mathematical discourse
redeploys

new_text.text: How literally does Deleuze take the calculus? Smith reads it as a model, and Voss as a source from which Deleuze extracts a philosophical concept of difference; Duffy traces a close correspondence between mathematical and philosophical concepts, though he too speaks of concepts “modelled on” mathematical theories, and his reviewer Evens objects that the reading pins philosophy to mathematical discourse; and Sokal and Bricmont, as Voss reports, doubted Deleuze’s grasp of the modern calculus.

claims.excerpt: structural correspondence
